imperial.name: Oriental Leaves

actions.text:
Sow

Late Jul–Aug for reliable outdoor leaves. Mizuna and mibuna also suit spring sowing. Shungiku Apr–Jul.

Plant out

Jul–Sep for the main crop. Earlier batches May–Jun.

methods.text:
Sow 

Use shallow drills or broadcast thinly for baby leaves. Use the depth for each type in Quick facts. Sow small batches. Give pak choi and Chinese cabbage more room when growing whole heads.

Plant out 

Raise seedlings in modules where pests or weeds make outdoor sowing difficult. Move plants before the roots are crowded. Keep the rootball intact and the crown clear. Water in well.

varieties.text:
Mizuna

Quick Japanese leaf with finely cut foliage and mild mustard flavour for salads or brief cooking.

Mibuna

Narrow, strap-like Japanese green. Use young leaves in salads, larger ones in stir-fries.

Red Frills mustard

Finely divided, peppery red mustard. Pick young and mix with milder salad leaves.

Joi Choi

Crisp white-stalked pak choi with green leaves. Pick young for salads, larger for stir-fries.

Tatsoi

Low rosettes of dark leaves for baby-leaf salads and quick cooking.

text:
Oriental Leaves.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Oriental leaves are quick salad and stir-fry crops, mostly brassicas: Chinese cabbage, leaf radish, mibuna, mizuna, mustards, pak choi and shungiku. Many give baby leaves within a month. Late-summer sowings often escape the worst flea beetle damage and fill the autumn salad gap; some leafy types crop into winter under cover. These tender, flavoursome greens are for fresh use, not long storage.

Quick facts
Sow

Late Jul–Aug for reliable outdoor leaves. Mizuna and mibuna also suit spring sowing. Shungiku Apr–Jul.

Plant out

Jul–Sep for the main crop. Earlier batches May–Jun.

Harvest

Aug – Nov

Sowing depth

Mizuna/mibuna, Chinese cabbage: about ½ in.; pak choi: ¾ in.; others: see packet.

Row spacing

Small-leaf: 10 in.; pak choi: 12 in.; Chinese cabbage: 18 in.

Plant spacing

Baby leaves: 4–6 in.; larger leaves: 8 in.; mature pak choi/cabbage hearts: 12 in.

Ready in

From sowing: baby leaves ~3–4 weeks; pak choi ~6; cabbage hearts ~10 weeks

Recommended varieties
Mizuna

Quick Japanese leaf with finely cut foliage and mild mustard flavour for salads or brief cooking.

Mibuna

Narrow, strap-like Japanese green. Use young leaves in salads, larger ones in stir-fries.

Red Frills mustard

Finely divided, peppery red mustard. Pick young and mix with milder salad leaves.

Joi Choi

Crisp white-stalked pak choi with green leaves. Pick young for salads, larger for stir-fries.

Tatsoi

Low rosettes of dark leaves for baby-leaf salads and quick cooking.

Key risks
Flea beetle

Flea beetles make small round holes in young brassica leaves, especially during warm, dry weather.

Slugs

Slugs chew leaves and seedlings, especially pak choi in damp conditions.

Bolting

Cold checks, long days, heat or drought can encourage premature flowering, depending on the species and variety.

Cabbage caterpillars

Chinese cabbage and other brassica leaves may be attacked by caterpillars.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
70
SALADS & LEAVES

Keep leaves tender.

Water regularly and avoid checks to growth.

Choose the right season.

Late-summer sowings suit most oriental brassica leaves.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil, with plenty of mature compost.
Clear earlier crops promptly and rake a fine seedbed. Keep late-summer sowings moist as they establish.
Sowing & planting
Raise small plugs
Keep the crown clear
Sow 

Use shallow drills or broadcast thinly for baby leaves. Use the depth for each type in Quick facts. Sow small batches. Give pak choi and Chinese cabbage more room when growing whole heads.

Plant out 

Raise seedlings in modules where pests or weeds make outdoor sowing difficult. Move plants before the roots are crowded. Keep the rootball intact and the crown clear. Water in well.

Looking after the crop
Water, weed, and thin or harvest crowded plants for fast, tender growth. Mesh susceptible brassicas against flea beetles and butterflies; late July/August sowings usually suffer less than spring/early summer.
Water Chinese cabbage generously and mulch around established plants, keeping centres clear. Let hearts form naturally.
Handle fragile-rooted pak choi gently; take small, regular pickings and remove damaged outer leaves. Keep ground clean against slugs. Pick shungiku shoots before flowering.
Harvesting & storage
Cut tender baby leaves about 1¼ in. above soil, keeping the growing point intact; water for regrowth. Cut rather than pick mibuna.
Pick individual leaves or whole plants according to the crop. Cut Chinese cabbage once hearts form, before damaging frost.
Mizuna and hardy mustards can give protected winter pickings. Leaf radish quality declines as winter approaches unless protected.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Flea beetle	Small round holes in young leaves.	Mesh brassica seedlings; keep growth steady.
Slugs	Chewed leaves, especially pak choi.	Hand-pick slugs; clear damaged outer leaves.
Bolting	Early flowering; poor leaves or hearts.	Sow in the right season; avoid drought and checks.
Cabbage caterpillars	Chewed leaves; eggs or larvae.	Cover with mesh; remove eggs and caterpillars.
Dryness and checks	Coarse leaves; poor hearts.	Water thoroughly, thin and mulch established plants.
Cabbage root fly	Tunnels in brassica roots.	Use mesh after sowing and rotate brassica crops.
Root disturbance	Plants loosen during picking.	Support pak choi while picking; handle roots gently.
Frost	Leaves damaged by cold weather.	Harvest tender heads; protect hardy winter leaves.
Final tips

Use close sowings for baby leaves; give hearts more room.

Small late-July and August batches spread autumn picking.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
See also: Vegetable Troubles 130–131 · Growing Techniques 171
71
